guide_enrichment.narrative:
Our model’s preference for Army starts with the ground game. Our efficiency numbers grade Army’s rushing offense as a major advantage against Florida Atlantic’s run defense. The early production supports that view: Army averaged 394 rushing yards through two games, all five first-listed offensive linemen were seniors, and the offense allowed only 0.5 sacks and 3.0 tackles for loss per game. For us, that combination points to a credible path for Army to control the game rather than relying on one recent result.

There is also enough of a passing constraint to keep Florida Atlantic from selling out completely against the run. Cale Hellums completed 9 of 10 passes for 91 yards and two touchdowns against South Florida. We are not treating that performance as a new baseline, but it matters when paired with Army’s rushing efficiency because it gives the offense another way to punish an overly aggressive defense.

The concern is on the other side. Our numbers rate Florida Atlantic well in both passing efficiency and creating scoring opportunities, while Army grades poorly at preventing those opportunities. That gives Florida Atlantic a realistic route to stay within the margin even if Army moves the ball consistently. We still make Army the stronger side, but the current price does not provide enough value for us to turn that disagreement into a wager.
guide_enrichment.matchup_to_watch:
We are watching Army’s rushing offense against Florida Atlantic’s run defense. Army had 25 rushing plays of at least 10 yards through three weeks, so this is not only an offense built around steady gains; it has also generated chunk plays. If Army continues creating those gains, it can dictate possession and limit Florida Atlantic’s chances to attack the weaker areas of Army’s defense.

That matchup explains our lean, but it also explains the pass. We need Army’s rushing advantage to translate into enough separation, not merely sustained drives. Florida Atlantic’s offensive profile leaves less room for error than the run-defense mismatch alone might suggest.

recent_game.fact: Army lost 28-24 to South Florida on Sept. 12, leaving the Black Knights 1-1 overall and 0-1 in the American Conference.
Against South Florida, Godspower Nwawuihe led Army with 20 carries and 98 rushing yards and scored a 10-yard fourth-quarter touchdown.
Against South Florida, Zach Mundell caught three passes, including a 24-yard touchdown, and completed a 37-yard pass to Godspower Nwawuihe.

quarterback.fact: Senior Cale Hellums was listed as Army's starting quarterback on the unofficial depth chart dated Sept. 20, with Bryson Luter second and Ethan Washington third.
Hellums returned as Army's starting quarterback in 2026 after making 10 starts and playing in every game in 2025.
Hellums rushed for 1,223 yards and 18 touchdowns in 2025; the 18 rushing touchdowns were the second-most in an Army season.
Against South Florida, Hellums completed 9 of 10 passes for 91 yards and two touchdowns, setting a career high with a .900 completion percentage.
Through two games in 2026, Hellums had 142 rushing yards, 150 passing yards and a team-high four total touchdowns.
Army had not thrown an interception through its first two games of 2026.

offensive_personnel.fact: Army's Sept. 20 offensive line listed Henry Appleton at left tackle, Kyle Kloska at left guard, Brady Small at center, Paolo Gennarelli at right guard and Teddy Williams at right tackle.
All five offensive linemen listed first on Army's Sept. 20 depth chart were seniors.
Army's first-listed skill personnel included running back Godspower Nwawuihe, slotback Samari Howard, H-back Brady Mott, tight end Parker Poloskey and wide receiver Brady Anderson.
Nwawuihe had emerged as Army's feature back after his performance in the 2025 Fenway Bowl.
Senior slotback Zach Mundell returned in 2026 after playing only one game since 2023 before the season opener; he rushed for 105 yards and two touchdowns on four carries against Bryant.
Through two games, Mundell led Army with 150 rushing yards, followed by Nwawuihe with 147 and Hellums with 142.

defensive_personnel.fact: Army's Sept. 20 defensive front listed Dillon Stowers at defensive tackle, Kody Harris-Miller at nose tackle and Jack Bousum at defensive end.
Army's first-listed linebackers were Noah Nixon at outside linebacker and Jaquavious Moss and Elijah Walton at inside linebacker.
Army's first-listed secondary consisted of nickel Zane Tallman, cornerbacks Jaydan Mayes and Jaxon Hammond, strong safety Caleb Williams and free safety Stephen Nnadozie.
Elijah Walton and Jaquavious Moss shared Army's team lead with 12 tackles apiece through two games.
Dillon Stowers led Army with one sack through two games, while Zane Tallman had the team's only forced fumble.

coaching_changes.fact: Jeff Monken was in his 13th season as Army's head coach in 2026.
Cody Worley remained Army's offensive coordinator and quarterbacks coach, while Daryl Dixon remained defensive coordinator and Scot Sloan served as co-defensive coordinator and safeties coach.
Army added first-year assistants John Holt as co-offensive line coach, Jamere Hogue as defensive line coach and Munir Prince as cornerbacks coach for 2026.

Army led the FBS in rushing offense at 394.0 yards per game through the first three weeks of 2026.

Army averaged 34:22 in time of possession through two games, ranking 10th nationally.
